articles.title: Six months of the Iran war – as told through Trump’s social media posts
articles.summary: How a war was announced, prosecuted, declared won, negotiated and then reopened, all in the president’s own words.
articles.body:
This week marks six months since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran.

In that time, US President Donald Trump has published at least 319 posts mentioning Iran on Truth Social, his social media platform – roughly one every 14 hours.

Read in sequence, these posts, or “truths” as they are known on the platform, form a record of how a war was announced, prosecuted, declared won, negotiated and then reopened, all in the president’s own words.

Al Jazeera analysed these posts. Here is what we found.

Between February 28 and August 25, Trump posted at least 4,189 times on Truth Social, an average of 24 posts a day, or one every hour. One in every 13 mentioned Iran – 319 posts in total, or one every 14 hours.

While he posted at all hours, the most common time for his Iran posts was the morning in Washington, between 8 and 11am (13:00-16:00 GMT), corresponding to early evening in Tehran.

The word cloud below provides a snapshot of the most commonly used terms. “Iran” dominates at 510 mentions, more than three times the next word. But the two that follow are not Iran’s leaders or its nuclear programme: they are his own name and his own country.

Trump refers to himself as “President Donald J Trump” or “President DJT” 221 times, more often than he mentions the Strait of Hormuz, nuclear weapons and Israel combined.

His sign-off, “Thank you for your attention to this matter”, closes one in every four posts.

In the weeks leading up to February 28, Iran was an occasional subject, appearing in 17 posts between January 1 and February 27, roughly one every three days.

The messaging blended hardline threats with transactional diplomacy. Trump applauded Iranian leadership for cancelling more than 800 scheduled hangings and expressed support for anti-regime protesters. He also threatened 25 percent tariffs on nations doing business with Iran, and repeatedly urged Tehran to negotiate, declaring: “MAKE A DEAL!”

Then, on January 28, he announced that “a massive Armada is heading to Iran”.

Over the next month, the messaging escalated the threat of force with several mentions of “Operation Midnight Hammer”, the US military operation of June 2025 that targeted and severely damaged Iranian nuclear enrichment facilities towards the end of the 12-day war with Israel.

On February 28 at 1:35am Eastern Time (06:35 GMT), US Central Command ( CENTCOM ) announced the commencement of Operation Epic Fury, at the direction of the president of the United States.

Fifty-five minutes later, at 07:30 GMT, US President Donald Trump posted an eight-minute video to Truth Social providing more details about the US’s “major combat operations” in Iran.

Later that evening, Trump posted: “Khamenei, one of the most evil people in History, is dead”, referring to Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had led the country since 1989.

Over the next two weeks, Trump posted 40 more times, arguing he was right to launch the strikes and ruling out any settlement short of “UNCONDITIONAL SURRENDER!”

The Strait of Hormuz, which would come to dominate the next five months, went unmentioned until March 10.

On March 13, Trump announced that CENTCOM had “totally obliterated every MILITARY target in Iran’s crown jewel, Kharg Island,” adding that he had chosen not to destroy the island’s oil infrastructure “for reasons of decency”.

March 14: ‘We have already destroyed 100% of Iran’s Military capability.’

Two weeks into the war, on March 14, Trump posted: “We have already destroyed 100% of Iran’s Military capability.”

Trump spent much of the rest of March and April cataloguing destruction and issuing deadlines to Iran.

He announced strikes on Kharg island , bridges and power plants, set 48-hour and 10-day ultimatums over the Strait of Hormuz, and repeated that Iran’s navy, air force and leadership were “gone”.

Between the threats, he attacked NATO, France, the United Kingdom, the Democrats – which he repeatedly calls “Dumocrats” – and the “fake news” media.

April 7: ‘A whole civilization will die tonight’

On April 7, Trump warned that “a whole civilization will die tonight”, as he announced a “final” strike on Iran. It never came. Ten hours and 26 minutes later, he said Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Field Marshal Asim Munir had asked him to hold off, and that he had agreed to a two-week ceasefire on condition that Iran reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

April 12: ‘BLOCKADING any and all Ships’

On the morning of April 12, Trump posted an article floating a naval blockade as the “Trump card the president holds if Iran won’t bend”. Hours later he announced one, writing, “the United States Navy, the Finest in the World, will begin the process of BLOCKADING any and all Ships trying to enter, or leave, the Strait of Hormuz.”

The naval blockade, which he later nicknamed “A WALL OF STEEL”, became the one instrument he never traded away.

April 20: ‘Israel never talked me into the war with Iran’

On April 20, Trump posted that “Israel never talked me into the war with Iran”.

For a war the two countries launched together, however, Israel is almost absent from his account of it, appearing just 32 times, fewer than in one in 10 posts. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is named just twice.

The following day, Pakistan asked Trump to extend the ceasefire. He agreed, but kept the blockade. Iran, he repeated, was losing $500m a day as a result of his blockade.

The next three weeks are mostly attrition. At about 4am on April 29, Trump posted that “Iran has just informed us that they are in a ‘State of Collapse'” and wanted the strait to be opened before posting an AI-generated image of himself holding an assault-style rifle.

May 3: ‘Project Freedom will begin Monday morning’

On May 3, Trump announced Project Freedom, a US Navy operation to escort ships from uninvolved countries out of the strait, before pausing it three days later “Based on the request of Pakistan and other Countries”.

Between May and June, the war became a negotiation, conducted in public.

On May 18, Trump said he had cancelled a planned attack at the request of Gulf leaders. Five days later, he posted from the Oval Office after a call with the same leaders as well as officials from Pakistan, Turkiye, Egypt, Jordan and Bahrain, negotiating a Memorandum of Understanding on peace. Israel was not on the call. Trump said he had spoken to Netanyahu separately.

For the next four weeks, the war is fought through the blockade rather than by air, with Trump setting out his terms on May 29 and later going on to describe Iran as a “FAILED NATION” unable to pay its own military.

On June 11, Trump promised to hit Iran “VERY HARD TONIGHT”, then cancelled a few hours later.

June 14: ‘The Deal with the Islamic Republic of Iran is now complete’

On June 14, Trump declared the agreement complete and told the world’s ships to start their engines. The same day, he criticised an Israeli strike on Beirut, saying it “should not have happened”.

The deal started fraying immediately. On June 26, in between two posts about how good his approval ratings were, Trump said Iran had fired at least four drones at ships in the Strait, one striking the deck of a cargo carrier.

Two days after that, US aircraft hit Iranian missile stores and coastal radar “for violating the Cease Fire Agreement, AGAIN!”. Trump ended his post by stating: “There may come a point when we are no longer able to be reasonable, and will be forced to militarily complete the job that we very successfully started. If that happens, the Islamic Republic of Iran will no longer exist! President DJT”.

On July 8, Trump posted an image of a fire at Chabahar in southeastern Iran, reposted from a pro-Israel open-source intelligence account, saying it was “in retribution for yesterday’s bombing of ships by Iran”.

On July 10, Trump wrote that the ceasefire was “OVER”. Three days later, the blockade returned – in his words, “we are reinstating the THE IRANIAN BLOCKADE”. On July 22, he set a rule: every time Iran shoots at a ship in the strait, the United States will destroy “ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT”. On August 2, he cancelled another planned attack, this time at the request of Iran and unnamed regional countries.

August 10: ‘Donald Trump Won the Iran War’

On August 10, Trump posted a link to an article with the headline, “Donald Trump Won the Iran War”.

Through August, the war has become an economic one. The 60-day memorandum of understanding expired with nothing to replace it; Trump said he would declare the Strait a US “territory” and, on August 19, he announced the “MOST CRUSHING ECONOMIC OPERATION EVER TAKEN AGAINST ANY COUNTRY”, threatening any nation that offers Iran a financial lifeline.

All told, across 32,478 words, six months of war reached the public one post at a time, in the president’s own words.

articles.title: Dolly Parton biopic, coffee brand and dog treats among star's upcoming business projects
articles.summary: "Dolly worked up until the day she died," her manager says, as her upcoming projects are revealed.
articles.body:
Singer and businesswoman Dolly Parton, who died earlier this week, had a slew of projects in the pipeline including a biopic, documentary, avatar show, museum, travel stop for truckers, coffee brand and dog treats.

"Dolly worked up until the day she died. She loved seeing her dreams come to life and loved knowing her work brought people joy," her longtime manager Danny Nozell told US media including Hollywood Reporter.

"If you see unreleased music, products, books, experiences and campaigns launched through official Dolly Parton channels, you can have confidence in knowing that she placed her personal stamp on it," he added.

Parton died peacefully in hospital in Nashville on 25 August after a "brief battle with cancer", after being admitted four days before her death with kidney and autoimmune issues.

Nozell said that Parton had worked with her "handpicked" team for the past several years, to "build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come".

The hugely successful and popular singer-songwriter and philanthropist took shrewd decisions throughout her career, which made her millions.

Just before her death, she told People on 21 August she was exploring new ways of touring, and that her team was collaborating with companies that create "avatar performances" given her recent health concerns.

She added they were in the "early stages of development", People said.

Dolly's Tennessean Travel Stops (celebrating National Truck Driver Appreciation Week)

Her Broadway show, Dolly: A True Original Musical, opens in December.

Harry Styles added his voice to the deluge of tributes for Parton, saying at his Madison Square Garden show she was "inspiration to his career". He also included her song I Will Always Love you as part of his show.

Meanwhile, flags across the US flew at half-mast on Wednesday, in tribute to the singer.

A family source has told news outlets that a private funeral service is due to take place this weekend in Nashville.

Last year, Parton said she had one song she couldn't talk about - it was still secret and buried in a vault in Dollywood , and will not be released until 2045.

"It's not supposed to be open 'til I'll be 100, and which, that's the day after tomorrow," Parton joked at the time.

How Dolly Parton's business savvy helped her succeed far beyond the charts

Maike Currie, vice-president of personal finance at savings firm PensionBee, told the BBC's Wake Up to Money that Parton had set examples for others.

She described her as a "brilliant businesswoman, but also an iconic investor and a real example to women about the power of what happens if women are financially independent".

Parton, who came from a humble, poor background in Tennessee, was always keen to encourage self-belief and confidence in others.

She wrote to the young recipients of books from Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, saying: "You and all of your friends are very special. There is no limit to what you can do or how far you can go.

"Just remember the lessons my family taught me - dream big dreams; learn everything you can learn; and care for all those who care for you. You do all of these things and you can be anyone you want to be."

articles.title: UK salmonella cases nearing 500 as egg investigations continue
articles.summary: Close to 500 people have become ill with salmonella linked to imported eggs, say UK authorities who are investigating more clusters.
articles.body:
Close to 500 people have become ill with salmonella linked to imported eggs, say UK authorities, who say they have identified two new clusters of the infection.

The UK Health Security Agency reported 207 cases last week. That has been increased to 259, with the two new clusters bringing the total to 474. There have been two deaths recorded.

Some of the cases date back a year, but all involve bacteria that are almost genetically identical, suggesting a common food source.

Investigations are ongoing, but based on what is known so far, experts say people have fallen sick after eating out rather than cooking eggs at home.

Cases of salmonella are being seen in other European countries too - Austria (2), Belgium (15), Denmark (1), France (4), Germany (6), the Netherlands (106).

Investigations in the Netherlands suggests a link with chicken meat, rather than eggs.

Salmonella can be found in a number of food sources including raw or under-cooked poultry or meat and eggs.

More than a third of those ill in the UK - some babies and others as old as 92 - have needed hospital care.

Most people get better without treatment, however.

While salmonella cases can happen any time, the UK outbreak involves a few specific, near-identical genetic clusters called t5.9411, t0.24068 and t5.9765.

259 confirmed cases and one death linked to t5.9411

38 confirmed cases and one death linked to t5.9765

177 confirmed cases linked to the t0.24068

Most have been recorded in recent weeks and months, but the investigations go back to cases as far as August 2025.

The majority have been in England, with many in London and Yorkshire and Humber.

There have been a small number of cases in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland too.

Preparing and cooking food thoroughly can prevent infection, as well as washing your hands after using the bathroom and before handling food.

It is safe to buy and eat eggs that have a British Lion mark or are produced under the Laid in Britain egg assurance scheme, experts advise.

Any suppliers of British Lion mark eggs have to stick to a strict code that covers testing and vaccinating hens against salmonella.

Prof Ian Young from the Food Standards Agency said: "We continue to work closely with the UK Health Security Agency and other partners to investigate.

"The exact causes of these outbreaks have not yet been identified, but investigations so far have identified links to imported eggs. There is no evidence that UK-produced eggs are affected."

The UKHSA said: "We will continue to follow up cases and investigate any further common sources if they come to light."

Symptoms include stomach cramps, diarrhoea, vomiting or fever. These usually develop between 12 and 72 hours after becoming infected.

Anyone who is concerned should contact their GP or out of hours service in the first instance, says the UKHSA.

In most cases people recover without further help but older people, babies and people with weakened immune systems are at greatest risk of severe disease.

articles.title: Glacier collapse may have caused Nepal floods and parents react to Meta settlement: Morning Rundown
articles.summary: Crews search for survivors after catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border.
articles.body: Crews search for survivors after catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border. Meta’s settlement in a social media addiction lawsuit is a first step toward a safer internet, parents say. Plus, a conservative TV network is planning MTV- and Bravo-inspired entertainment shows. Here’s what to know today. At least 270 dead after flooding on Nepal-Tibet border wipes out whole towns At least 270 people have been killed and hundreds more are missing after catastrophic flash floods swept through towns and valleys along the border between Nepal and China’s Tibet region, leaving ruins in their wake. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. Videos show crowds trying to flee a surging wall of mud, rows of buses and trucks swept aside like toys, and bridges cracked apart and swept away. Peaceful, lush green valleys are transformed in an instant. More than 500 foreigners from 32 countries are among those still unaccounted for in the rugged mountainous region, which is popular with pilgrims and trekkers. They include 65 people from the U.S. Chinese officials said three people were dead, two had been rescued and 558 people were missing after a mudslide at a land crossing in Tibet’s Gyirong county, including 260 foreign nationals. It was not immediately clear whether China and Nepal were counting some of the same people. The true scale of the casualties may take days to become clear, with power and communication lines swept away in some areas. An ice and rock avalanche from a high-altitude glacier may have triggered the flooding, with a large volume of debris entering the Lende Khola tributary, researchers have said in a preliminary assessment. Experts are also examining whether the jolt as the avalanche hit the river may have caused the 4.4-magnitude earthquake recording observed by the U.S. Geological Survey yesterday. USGS later updated the event, saying it was a 5.2-magnitude glacial collapse. Follow our live blog for the latest updates. Judge allows Trump’s mail-in ballots plan to proceed A federal judge lifted a nationwide injunction yesterday on President Donald Trump’s executive order on mail-in ballots, allowing him to move forward, at least temporarily, with his effort to exert federal control over the practice ahead of the midterm elections. The decision comes after a Supreme Court decision on Monday favored Trump in a similar case. Trump’s executive order directs the U.S. Postal Service to track mail-in ballots and potentially reject those submitted by people not on a federal list of eligible voters, which conflicts with states’ traditional role in administering elections. There remains a strong chance that key aspects of the executive order will be blocked at some stage, possibly as soon as this week. More on the legal challenges to Trump’s order. More politics news: The man accused of being the mastermind behind the 9/11 attacks will stand trial starting in June 2028. The Secret Service’s communications director and two other agency officials have been placed on leave amid an investigation into potential misconduct. Meta’s settlement a first step toward safer internet, parents say Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, has agreed to an $18 billion settlement in a wide-ranging social media addiction lawsuit with the state of California and several other states. The deal establishes two-hour daily limits and blocks nighttime use for teen users, hides likes on teens’ posts and blocks what the company called “extreme makeup filters.” Here’s what else Meta agreed to. Parents who spoke to NBC News said they see the settlement as just a first step in an industry they say has prioritized engagement and growth over young users’ safety and well-being. “One part of me is proud, and the other part is thinking: When are we going to actually hold someone accountable?” said one mother whose 16-year-old son died by suicide after, the family said, he was targeted in a social media sextortion scheme. Another mom, who lost her 17-year-old daughter to fentanyl poisoning after a drug dealer she met on Instagram sold her counterfeit Percocet, said she is skeptical. “That’s all part of their PR plan,” she said. Here’s what other parents said about the deal. Tim Curry, star of ‘Rocky Horror Picture Show,’ dies at 80 Just a day after the passing of country music star Dolly Parton, the world is mourning the loss of another pop culture icon: Tim Curry. The British actor died peacefully at his Los Angeles home at age 80, his representatives said. Co-stars from “Clue” and “Home Alone 2” paid tribute to his illustrious career. A post on the Muppets’ social media page called Curry, who starred in “Muppet Treasure Island,” one of the few humans who “earned the title of honorary Muppet.” But the actor was perhaps best known for his memorable role as Dr. Frank-N-Furter in 1975’s “The Rocky Horror Picture Show.” Curry had long been dealing with health issues following a 2012 stroke that left him partially paralyzed and unable to walk. In one of his last on-camera interviews, he reflected on how acting gave him “the freedom of being somebody else.” Read more about Curry’s life and career. Remembering Dolly Parton: In the Tennessee county that Dolly Parton called home, courthouse bells tolled, students observed a moment of silence and fans flocked to Dollywood. Here’s how Pigeon Forge paid homage to its most famous resident. Parton’s legacy of literacy lives on in a small English town. How Parton showed love to the LGBTQ community and what her support meant to them. Staff Pick: MTV for MAGA: Conservative network plans new entertainment The TV network home to Steve Bannon’s “War Room” and “The Charlie Kirk Show” is trying something new: an entertainment slate inspired by channels like MTV, Bravo and VH-1 that aims to give viewers something different to the political news that has traditionally been the company’s bread and butter. For anyone who grew up in that era, the planned line-up of Real America’s Voice will have some familiar echoes. There’s “Left Right Love,” a dating series that will bring together liberals and conservatives, and a talent competition with a working title of “Star Spangled Talent.” And RAV will also expand into music programming with “Real America’s Music LIVE,” a nod to MTV’s era-defining, “Total Request Live,” and the flagship program for its forthcoming Real America’s Music channel. The expansion comes as pro-Trump media faces headwinds and the broader industry runs into changing viewer habits. But Real America’s Voice is betting its unusually loyal audience can follow it beyond political news. So I wanted to know more about what’s next for Real America’s Voice and why executives believe an audience built around politics will stick around for something different. — Katherine Doyle, national security reporter Read All About It Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese avant-garde artist renowned for her immersive mirror rooms and polka dots, has died at age 97. A near-total lunar eclipse will be visible across the U.S. tonight. Here’s the best time to see it. The FDA approved a groundbreaking pancreatic cancer drug that experts predict will transform treatment for the disease. Blake Lively can recover about $400,000 in legal fees over Justin Baldoni’s dismissed defamation lawsuit against her, a judge ruled. For subscribers: A man known as “The Defendant” locked up for stealing a dead teen’s identity. The feds still don’t know his name. NBC Selected: Online Shopping, Simplified Hurricane season is here, so the NBC Selected staff spoke to a meteorologist about what to prep ahead of a storm and how to stay safe if one makes landfall. We also spoke with a doctor about what to know about West Nile virus, including the products that will help keep you protected. Sign up to The Selection newsletter for hands-on product reviews, expert shopping tips and a look at the best deals and sales each week. Thanks for reading today’s Morning Rundown. articles.title: Lucky Charms and Trix go au naturel as General Mills ditches artificial colors
articles.summary: General Mills said Wednesday it has removed artificial colors from all its U.S. cereals, including Lucky Charms and Trix.
articles.body: General Mills said Wednesday it has removed artificial colors from all its U.S. cereals, including Lucky Charms and Trix. The Minneapolis company has shifted to fruit- and vegetable-based dyes as well as colors derived from spices like turmeric and paprika to give its cereals their customary bright colors. “This achievement reflects how we are evolving with consumer needs while continuing to offer food that tastes great, delivers quality and provides value,” said Bethany Quam, General Mills’ president of cereal, in a statement. General Mills said 90% of its U.S. retail products are now free of artificial dyes. Products that still contain artificial colors, like some Betty Crocker cake mixes and Fruit Roll-Ups, will transition to natural dyes by the end of 2027, the company said. General Mills is the second big cereal maker to announce a transition to natural dyes. WK Kellogg, which makes Froot Loops and Apple Jacks, said earlier this month that it will remove artificial colors from all its U.S. cereals by the end of this year. Health advocates have long called for the removal of artificial dyes from foods, citing studies indicating they can cause neurobehavioral problems, including hyperactivity and attention issues, in some children, though the findings have been mixed. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration says approved dyes are safe and that “most children have no adverse effects” from them. But the agency says some children may be sensitive to artificial dyes. Last year, the FDA banned one petroleum-based dye, Red 3, because some studies suggested it caused cancer in lab rats. General Mills removed artificial dyes from Trix in 2015 but brought them back two years later, saying U.S. customers missed the bright colors. But pressure from consumers and politicians has grown since then. President Donald Trump’s health secretary, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., has urged food companies to phase out petroleum-based artificial dyes. Last summer, General Mills signed an agreement with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton saying it would remove synthetic dyes from all its products by the end of 2027. Retailers are also forcing companies to act. Earlier this year, Target said it would stop selling cereals that contain artificial colors by the end of May. Walmart has also said it will remove artificial colors from its store brands by January 2027.

articles.title: Small plane crashes in water next to remote Alaska coastal town, killing all 4 on board
articles.summary: A small plane carrying four people crashed into shallow waters next to a remote coastal town in Alaska on Wednesday, killing everyone on board, according to officials.
articles.body: A small plane carrying four people crashed into shallow waters next to a remote coastal town in Alaska on Wednesday, killing everyone on board, according to officials. The Piper PA-24 was heading for the airport in the small town of Seldovia after taking off from Anchorage, according to a statement from the Alaska Department of Public Safety. Seldovia’s airport is about 136 miles (219 kilometers) southwest of Anchorage. After it crashed, it was submerged in about 15 feet (4.6 meters) of water in the Seldovia Slough near the shore, said Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief. Troopers had to wait until the tide went out in order to reach it. Troopers were able to get the bodies of the four adults out of the plane. They’re being sent to the medical examiner’s office and their names will not be released until next of kin are notified, according to the Department of Public Safety. It was not immediately clear what may have caused the crash. The NTSB is investigating. U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, of Alaska, said he’ll be getting a briefing from the NTSB and Federal Aviation Administration as they work to figure out what went wrong. “These tragedies are heartbreaking and unacceptable, which is why aviation safety and infrastructure in Alaska continue to be a top focus of mine,” he said in a post on Facebook. Less than a week earlier, another plane crashed at a remote military site in western Alaska, killing all eight people on board. The aircraft had been making its second runway approach in heavy fog and its pilots could not see the gravel airstrip, authorities said.

articles.title: Satellite images show destruction from Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: A glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday triggered catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border.
articles.body:
At least 359 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,300 remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after a Himalayan glacier collapse sent a wall of water, mud and rock through border towns and valleys.

Rescue teams are searching for survivors in terrain that is hard to access at the best of times. At least 19 bridges and about 40km (25 miles) of road have been destroyed, further hampering the search.

Nepal Police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle said the death toll is expected to rise further.

Satellite imagery captured by Planet Labs before and after the flood shows how buildings and roads have been washed away.

The imagery also shows large parts of Syapru Besi village submerged in mud.

At about 8:40am local time (02:55 GMT) on Wednesday, a large section of glacier broke away high above the Lhende river in Tibet. The falling ice and rock dammed the river and, shortly afterwards, when the blockage gave way, the surge tore through settlements in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, destroying homes, hydropower plants and border infrastructure.

The resulting ice and rock avalanche struck the river about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.

Early reports attributed the collapse to a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. But the United States Geological Survey later said the seismic signal was caused by the landslide itself, not an earthquake. The landslide packed enough force to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.

Some of the worst damage was in Rasuwa district, on Nepal’s northern border with China. The surge travelled down the Lhende Khola (river) into the Bhotekoshi and then the Trishuli river, which rose by as much as 9 metres (30 feet) in 30 minutes, according to Nepali officials.

Timure and Syapru Besi were among the settlements hit in Rasuwa. Further downstream, the flooding reached parts of Nuwakot and Dhading. Bodies have since been recovered much further south, in Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan and the two Nawalparasi districts.

In Tibet, mud and debris struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse.

The Trishuli eventually joins the Narayani, which flows into India’s Bihar state, where it is known as the Gandak.

articles.title: Experts zero in on likely cause of deadly Nepal mudslide, with more than 1,400 missing
articles.summary: A massive glacier collapse triggered a magnitude 5.2 landslide event that caused catastrophic Nepal and Tibet floods, with over 1,400 people still missing.
articles.body: The catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet now estimated to have killed hundreds were likely triggered by a massive glacier collapse and debris flow that registered as a magnitude 5.2 landslide, according to the U.S. Geological Service (USGS). The USGS originally pinpointed the cause of the mudslides as a 4.4 magnitude earthquake but later updated its analysis after observing data from nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves and satellite imagery. That data suggested that no earthquake had occurred. Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development told The Associated Press that Wednesday’s flash floods were likely triggered by a glacial avalanche. "Hydrological observations indicate the exceptional speed and magnitude of the flood wave," they said in a statement, adding that at one point, the water levels on the Trishuli River rose by as much as 27 feet in just a half hour. TERRIFYING VIDEO CAPTURES PEOPLE FLEEING INCOMING MUDSLIDE AT NEPAL-CHINA BORDER The death toll has climbed to more than 360 people estimated to have been killed in the floods along the Nepal-China border, the AP reported, citing local police. Rescue teams are now searching for the more than 1,400 people who went missing during the chaos. Many of them were foreigners and pilgrims. Nepal Police on Thursday began posting lists of Nepali and foreign nationals missing. Several dozen Americans were listed. A U.S. State Department spokesperson confirmed to Fox News that as of 8 a.m. Thursday, there are approximately 90 Americans who may have been impacted by the floods. The U.S. embassies in Nepal and China are working to assist Americans in affected areas. "The State Department is closely monitoring the situation and has deployed a disaster response advisor to the region to support response efforts," the spokesperson said. "The Department will also provide $500,000 in assistance through its global award with Catholic Relief Services, supporting emergency shelter, relief items, and water, sanitation, and hygiene assistance to flood-affected communities in Nepal." The Nepalese army rescued more than 100 people from flood-hit areas by helicopter Thursday morning, according to army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Raja Ram Basnet. BABY PULLED FROM VEHICLE TRAPPED IN RAGING FLOODWATERS IN DRAMATIC RESCUE CAUGHT ON VIDEO The flooding destroyed dozens of bridges and nearly 25 miles of roads, further complicating search and rescue efforts, according to Nepalese officials. Bishal Kumar Bhandari, chairman of the Nepal Red Cross Society, told the AP that they have shifted focus to large-scale relief operations. He said that around 1,200 people were displaced from at least three villages. Videos of the disaster showed raging floodwaters sweeping away cars, engulfing people trying to flee and destroying homes and bridges. Debris was left tangled in tree branches and power lines, vehicles were buried and mud-covered survivors emerged as flooding cut off travel in some areas. The village of Soley in Nuwakot, which has about 25 homes, was almost entirely destroyed, according to Kathmandu-based journalist Nirajan Paudyal, whose parents and other relatives live there. Desperate for news, he traveled to the area Thursday to check on his family. "There is no update till now. I fear there won’t be any update," Paudyal told the AP. 11 VISITORS TRAPPED AS DANGEROUS FLASH FLOODING TEARS THROUGH ICONIC NATIONAL PARK The Dalai Lama, the highest spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism, released a message to those affected by the floods in the region. "I am saddened to learn of the devastating floods in the Rasuwa region of Nepal and Kyirong in Tibet, resulting in loss of life and heavy structural damage," the 91-year-old leader said in a statement. "I pray for all those who have lost their lives, and offer my sympathy and heartfelt condolences to the bereaved and to all those affected by this tragedy." He continued: "Since this region has seen calamities in the past as well, these are certainly symptoms of a deeper underlying cause — whether climate change or other factors. I hope that appropriate follow-up measures will be taken, wherever possible, to help ensure that such disasters do not recur." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The disaster in Nepal and Tibet underscores a broader threat, as increasingly unstable Himalayan ice poses risks to communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region experienced similar flash flooding in August 2025, when high temperatures caused a glacial lake in Tibet to overflow. The resulting floods killed nine people and damaged critical infrastructure, including a bridge linking Nepal and China.

articles.title: Thieves raid bronze age collection in ‘super-fast’ Spain museum heist
articles.summary: It is not immediately known how many of the 50-plus mainly gold objects from the Treasure of Villena were taken.
articles.body:
Thieves have raided the Treasure of Villena, one of the greatest Bronze Age gold collections, in the latest high-profile heist on a European museum, officials said.

It was not immediately known how many of the 50-plus mainly gold objects in the collection were taken in the heist on Thursday, as police were still making an inventory, a spokesperson for the council in the Spanish town of Villena said.

“The alarm at the Villena Museum went off around 5:20am,” said the spokesperson, adding that by 5:24am the thieves had left the building.

The operation was “super-fast and super-professional”, he added.

The 29 bracelets, 11 bowls, three bottles, and other miscellaneous pieces in the Treasure of Villena are kept in a small museum in the Alicante province town.

Though mainly of gold, there are also pieces of silver, iron and amber, all dating back to about 1,000 BC. The treasure was discovered in 1963 by archaeologist Jose Maria Soler in a vessel sunk in a dried-out riverbed in Villena.

“All security systems were activated,” according to the Villena spokesman, who insisted there had been “no failure” by the museum.

Shortly before the robbery, another alarm went off at the city’s sports centre, and authorities were investigating whether that was a diversion created by the thieves, the spokesperson added.

There have been a series of brazen raids of institutions across Europe in recent months.

Last October, thieves broke into the Louvre Museum in Paris in broad daylight, escaping in less than eight minutes with jewellery worth $102m.

And earlier this month, four works “of extraordinary value” by Renaissance artist Antonello da Messina were stolen from a museum in Sicily , Italy’s Ministry of Culture said.

Also this month, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m that were stolen from the Magnani-Rocca Foundation museum near Parma earlier this year.

articles.title: I was told I should not be at the National Eisteddfod, says Reform MS
articles.summary: Helen Jenner said she was criticised for attending the festival because of her membership of her party.
articles.body:
An MS has said she has faced criticism for attending the National Eisteddfod because she is a member of Reform.

The party's deputy Welsh leader, Helen Jenner, said online commenters said she had no right to be at the Welsh language festival because of her membership of the right-wing party.

Jenner, who grew up on Anglesey, said the criticism was ridiculous but that it didn't bother her.

She made the comments to the BBC Wales political podcast, Walescast .

"I see the odd comment [online], surprisingly, from some quite professional people making remarks about me."

She said a recent comment had claimed she had "no right to be in the Eisteddfod, because I'm in Reform, I had no right to be there, and that it was a disgrace that I was there speaking Welsh".

"You know, a lot of, I will be honest, Plaid Cymru, Yes Cymru supporters being very annoyed at the fact that I portray myself as a Welsh person because apparently, you know, you can't be Welsh-speaking in Reform.

"So, I get bits like that, but it doesn't bother me. I just think it's ridiculous."

Separately, Jenner said she is concerned for the safety of her own family after the death of Ann Widdecombe .

"What happened to Ann Widdecombe was so horrifying I don't even think I fully processed it.

"Because I think if I fully actually engaged with the nature of what happened I would just be in a bit of a state.

"I am concerned about... my family, I'm concerned about other members.

"I want my home to be secure but one thing it hasn't done is put me off. It has made me more determined to determine to carry on."

Jenner is the party's spokesperson on education and the Welsh language.

On the latter topic, she said she thinks the Welsh government needs a "different approach".

Despite the target for a million Welsh speakers, she said: "Something is kind of going wrong because there are fewer people at the moment, the uptick is a bit lower.

"I just think we need to look at it again, because what's the point in having that target if it's achieving the opposite?"

The 2021 census had shown a reduction in the percentage of Welsh speakers to 17.8%, which was approximately 538,000 residents aged three or older in Wales saying they can speak Welsh.

Jenner, a former teacher, said she wanted to see more Welsh-speaking teachers go into the education system and deliver a bilingual education.

"From my personal experience that is where a lot of youngsters get their Welsh and are able to... learn Welsh properly".

articles.title: Ratko Mladić, ex-Bosnian Serb warlord who oversaw atrocities in Bosnia, dies in prison at 84
articles.summary: Ratko Mladić, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in a U.N.-designated “safe area” of Bosnia, Europe’s worst atrocity since World War Two, has died, a U.N. ​official said on Thursday.
articles.body: Ratko Mladić, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in a U.N.-designated “safe area” of Bosnia, Europe’s worst atrocity since World War Two, has died, a U.N. ​official said on Thursday. Mladić, who was serving a life sentence on charges of genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes, died in a U.N. prison hospital in The Hague, Netherlands, a spokesperson confirmed. A U.N. statement said that Dutch authorities “have commenced the standard procedures and investigations required under Dutch national law,” while Judge Graciela Gatti Santana of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals has “ordered a full inquiry.” The slaughter in Srebrenica was the grisly culmination of a war that had lasted over three years, in which the general pounded the besieged capital Sarajevo daily with the artillery, tanks, mortars and heavy machine guns of his nationalist Serb army, killing 10,000. The dead from Srebrenica were bulldozed into mass graves over four days in July 1995, some of them dug up and relocated to remote mountains so as to hide evidence of the killings. The goal, as determined by the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia (ICTY), was “ethnic cleansing” — the ⁠forcible expulsion of Bosnian Muslims, Croats and other non-Serbs to clear Bosnian lands for a Greater Serbia. The tribunal found that Mladić, together with late Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic and Bosnian Serb political leader Radovan Karadzic, were part of a criminal conspiracy to implement the plan. “I do not recognise this court,” Mladić, dubbed the “Butcher of Bosnia” by his opponents, said at an ICTY hearing on his case in 2014. When he was sentenced to life in prison in 2017 he shouted: “This is all lies, you are all liars!” According to his son, documents gave Mladić’s date of birth at March 12, 1942, but he was actually born on March 8, 1943. Genocide conviction Karadzic, also convicted of genocide in 2016, ⁠and Mladić topped the ICTY wanted list for years after Western powers ended the war. But until Milosevic was toppled ​by ⁠a popular uprising in 2000, Mladić lived securely - if discreetly - in Belgrade. Milosevic died in detention on March 11, 2006, a few months before a verdict in his four-year tribunal trial for genocide and other war crimes in Croatia, Bosnia and Kosovo. The army Mladić created to fight in Bosnia was a model of ruthlessness, daring and brutality in the Serb warrior tradition, once prized ⁠in the life-or-death partisan struggle against the Nazi occupation of Yugoslavia in World War Two. In some of the most horrific examples, prisoners suffocated in the heat after being forced to eat salt ​and denied water; were starved ⁠and raped in prison camps; were made to jump off a bridge and ‌shot; and were gunned down at night by the hundreds after being driven out of detention with chemical gas. “For me Mladić is a symbol of all horrible crimes that happened during the war - our girls were raped, and boys killed, only because they were Muslim,” said Munira Subasic, whose son and husband were killed by Bosnian Serb forces after they overran Srebrenica. “Germans had Hitler, Serbs have Mladić,” Subasic continued. “There ‌is no difference between the two.” Mladić had a cameraman film the blitz on the encircled enclave of Srebrenica, to show ‌him extolling his “lads” and haranguing Dutch U.N. peacekeepers who misguidedly accepted his solemn word that the inhabitants would be safe in his hands. Srebrenica supposedly had “safe area” status, meant to protect civilians from ethnic cleansing. “We give this town to the Serb people as a gift,” Mladić said to the camera, claiming the victory as revenge against Muslim Turks, who once held the area as part of the Ottoman Empire. The next day, Mladić’s forces were filmed handing out sweets to children, promising their safe passage. Meanwhile, thousands of men and boys were being readied for ⁠execution. When NATO tried in 1995 to rein in his forces with the threat of limited air strikes, his troops defiantly seized U.N. peacekeepers as human shields, chaining them to likely targets. In November 1996 Mladić and top generals gave in to strong Western pressure that he step down as ordered by Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic, who succeeded Karadzic and was later jailed for her role in war crimes. Son of partisan fighter The son of a World War Two partisan fighter killed in 1945, Mladić was an officer in the old communist Yugoslav People’s Army (JNA) when Yugoslavia’s disintegration began in 1991. When Bosnian Serbs rose in 1992 against Bosnia’s Muslim-led secession, Mladić was picked to command the new Bosnian Serb army that swiftly overran 70% of the landlocked country. Dozens of towns were besieged with heavy weapons that once belonged to the JNA and villages were burned down as 22,000 troops of the U.N. Protection Force stood by more or less helplessly, with orders not to take sides. A combination of Western pressure, covert American arms and training for Croats and Muslims gradually ‌turned the tide against Mladić’s army. Determined NATO strikes did the rest. Sick and frail Despite Western appeals, the reformists ruling Serbia after Milosevic’s fall did not dare move against a man ​who was a hero to a core of nationalist Serbs. Sporadic sightings put him at a Belgrade horse race or a soccer match. In 2004, NATO said he had toasted hard-drinking old comrades ‌at his former bunker in Han Pijesak, Bosnia. When he was finally arrested in 2011, ⁠he put up no resistance. His right arm was lame, the apparent result of an untreated stroke. He looked nothing like the burly general in camouflage who ruffled the hair of a ⁠Srebrenica boy in 1995. He suffered a heart attack in 2013 and seemed older than his years. By his own account, he felt like a frail old man. In his few court appearances, he wavered between self-pity, smiling defiance and vague distraction. “I am a very sick ‌man,” Mladić pleaded to the court. In 2019, Mladić told the ​judges that he was too ill to participate in outdoor exercises and requested leave to visit the graves ‌of family members in Serbia. The request was denied. His appeal against conviction was rejected ​in 2021, as were repeated requests for his release on compassionate grounds. In August 2026, a UN doctor found Mladić’s death “may occur at any time,” possibly within weeks, but his application for release was again rejected as not in the interests of justice.

articles.title: Nepal floods: What caused the catastrophe, and what could happen next
articles.summary: South Asia News: A catastrophic flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district on Wednesday, killing and displacing hundreds of people and destroying bridges and other in.
articles.body: A catastrophic flood swept through Nepal’s Rasuwa district on Wednesday, killing and displacing hundreds of people and destroying bridges and other infrastructure along the Bhotekoshi river corridor.The death toll from the massive flash floods has risen to at least 353, police said.Bodies have since been recovered from Rasuwa and neighbouring districts, including Nuwakot, Dhading, Chitwan, Tanahun, Gorkha and Nawalparasi East, as scientists and climate experts investigate the cause of the sudden torrent.What caused the catastrophe?Scientists investigating the cause of the flash floods believe a glacier-related avalanche may have triggered the sudden surge of water.Analysis of satellite imagery indicates that a large mass of ice and rock may have fallen into a river, temporarily blocking its flow and creating a natural dam that later breached, sending floodwaters downstream, as cited by the Kathmandu Post.The US Geological Survey recorded a magnitude 4.4 earthquake in Tibet at 8.37 am Nepal time on Wednesday, around 47 kilometres north of Gosainkunda. Scientists have not yet determined whether the tremor triggered or contributed to the avalanche.The Nepali Times reported that an avalanche struck the northern face of Langtang Lirung, a 7,245-metre peak. The mountain was also involved in a major avalanche during the 2015 earthquake, when a slide on its southern face buried Langtang village and killed around 300 people.Experts from the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development said water levels in the Trishuli river rose by as much as nine metres within 30 minutes.The Lhende Khola, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi, was the worst affected, they said, as reported by the Kathmandu Post.The area was already considered vulnerable to sudden flooding. On July 8 last year, the Bhotekoshi river recorded another abrupt surge, which Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology attributed to a glacial lake outburst in the Lhende river near the Nepal-China border.Scientists have previously warned that the wider Himalayan region is home to numerous potentially dangerous glacial lakes.However, there had been no specific warning or forecast of an ice-and-rock avalanche at the location affected by Wednesday’s disaster.What happens nextScientists have not ruled out the possibility of further flooding or other hazards in the affected area.Home minister Sudan Gurung said on Wednesday afternoon that the Lhende river had not yet fully cleared.Rijan Bhakta Kayastha, a climate researcher and professor at Kathmandu University, said on Thursday that there had initially been concerns that another large body of water could have formed upstream.However, he said there was not yet enough evidence to confirm the existence of such a lake.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Finchley teacher of indecent assaults against two pupils
articles.summary: Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, was convicted at Harrow Crown Court of seven counts of indecent assault.
articles.body:
A chemistry teacher has been found guilty of indecently assaulting two teenage pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s.

Sally-Anne Bowen, who taught at Christ's College in Finchley, north London, assaulted the boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s.

On Thursday, a jury at Harrow Crown Court found the 65-year-old guilty of seven counts of indecent assault after deliberating for six hours and 29 minutes.

One complainant told the court he had sex with the teacher "about 20 or 30 times" over several months. He said he visited her at home, considered her his girlfriend and had fallen in love with her.

The man, who cannot be named for legal reasons, told the court she had "drummed it" into him that he must not tell anyone about them and to keep it a secret.

A second complainant told jurors he had kissed Bowen in a café after being "goaded" into it by other boys.

A former pupil at the school, Tobias Oliver, said during the trial that she acted like she was in "a Sabrina Carpenter video" while in the classroom and "dressed and behaved more like my teenage female friends than the other teachers".

"The topics of conversation in class often strayed away from chemistry and became quite sexual," said Oliver, who did not know the complainants.

He recalled incidents where Bowen flashed her underwear to a class while sitting on a table and went through and discussed a "sex manual" a student had brought in, which Oliver believed to be the Kama Sutra, with the class.

Richard Luker, who was head of science at the school in the late 1980s, told the court he remembered receiving a complaint from the first alleged victim's mother after she was worried that her son was planning to travel abroad with Bowen at the end of term.

During the trial, Bowen claimed the allegations were a "total fabrication" and that she had a medical condition which had not been diagnosed in the late 1980s and made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her.

Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, was granted bail.

articles.title: UEFA preps criminal complaint against FIFA’s Infantino over World Cup sell-off deal
articles.summary: UEFA is preparing a criminal complaint against FIFA President Gianni Infantino in Swiss courts for possible financial mismanagement over his failed plan to sell future World Cup profits to private investors.
articles.body: MONACO — The governing body for soccer in Europe is preparing a criminal complaint against FIFA President Gianni Infantino in Swiss courts for possible financial mismanagement over his failed plan to sell future World Cup profits to private investors. The Union of European Football Associations, or UEFA, said Thursday it filed documents in a Manhattan court requesting discovery of potential evidence from the New York investment fund, Thrive Capital Management, founded by Joshua Kushner, the younger brother of President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. UEFA also filed a request in a southern Florida district for authorization of discovery “in a foreign proceeding” against FIFA itself, which has offices in the Miami suburb of Coral Gables. Thrive and Kushner were to be the anchor investors intending to pay FIFA $4.2 billion for a 20% stake in a subsidiary that would run the soccer body’s commercial events, including the World Cup. “UEFA and its counsel are contemplating a Swiss criminal proceeding against Infantino and possibly other FIFA officials for criminal mismanagement under Article 158 of the Swiss Criminal Code,” UEFA’s lawyers state in a 56-page document seen by The Associated Press. The document suggests the $4.2 billion figure could be a “fraudulently off-market price promoted by Infantino for his own benefit.” Infantino dropped the sell-off plan on Aug. 1 after a furious backlash by global soccer leaders, including UEFA.

articles.title: Florida couple declared dead in helicopter crash in Kenya; thieves break in their house, steal Porsche, Land Rover in less than 24 hours. Then comes a twist in court
articles.summary: US News: 55-year-old Henry Parra and 42-year-old Adam Hlavaty, a same-sex couple from Florida, were among the seven people who were killed when a helicopter th.
articles.body: 55-year-old Henry Parra and 42-year-old Adam Hlavaty, a same-sex couple from Florida, were among the seven people who were killed when a helicopter they were in while on a safari in Kenya crashed last Wednesday. In less than 24 hours after they were declared dead and the news spread in their Florida neighborhood, thieves broke into the house of the couple and stole valuable works of art, jewelry, electronics, personal and business documents, apart from the couple's Land Rover and Porsche SUV.According to Coral Gables police, 40-year-old Geybert Alexander Garcia and 24-year-old Melany Perdomo ransacked the home. Police said a ping from the couple's stolen MacBook led investigators to Garcia and Perdomo.Both face multiple charges, including burglary and grand theft auto. Both suspects appeared before a judge, and they were held without bond.Miami-Dade Circuit Court Judge Mindy Glazer found probable cause for the charges and ordered them to stay away from the Coral Gables home.In court, a family friend testified about the damage that the suspects left behind at the home.She said the security system was broken into and the front door was also left with extensive damage that the family has to replace, including the front lock.'He was given authorization to use the vehicles'"Your honor, you'll see that the defendant's got prior felony convictions for burglarizing homes, money laundering, dealing in stolen property," a prosecutor said during Garcia's hearing, as reported by NBC Miami. "I don't know if this home was specifically targeted because I believe it was in the media that the victims passed away."Garcia's defense attorney, Paul Basile, provided a notarized document he said came from Garcia's family that they said was from one of the alleged victims. The document allegedly granted Garcia possession of their vehicles and entrance into their home, the attorney said."Oh I gotta see this," Judge Mindy Glazer said. "Really? Before they went on their vacation, they decided to give Mr Garcia authorization to use their vehicles, Mr Garcia, who has a criminal history?""Judge, I can only go by the information that's provided by the family," Basile responded."Yeah, I would not give that much weight," Glazer said."It's my understanding that the notary is actually a friend of the victim," Basile said."I'm not going to address anything until I hear from the officers for the probable cause hearing," Glazer responded. "But I mean, it's pretty egregious to break into somebody's home of victims who had just perished. So I'll consider whatever you ask based on what there's probable cause for."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills ‘newlywed’ woman in south Lebanon, wounds others
articles.summary: Violence has eased since the US-Iran MoU and Israel-Lebanon framework, but Beirut still reports strikes and demolitions.
articles.body:
A Lebanese woman has been killed, and several other people injured by Israeli strikes on the town of Arab Salim, in southern Lebanon’s Nabatieh district.

Lebanon’s Ministry of Health said six people were wounded in the attacks on Thursday, including a child, a woman and two elderly people, while the state-run National News Agency (NNA) reported that the woman who died “had been married for 48 hours”.

The newlywed woman’s house was also destroyed in the attack, NNA said.

Lebanese security sources said at least 10 Israeli strikes had been carried out in the wider Nabatieh area. NNA also reported artillery shelling targeting the outskirts of the town of Rashaf in the Bint Jbeil district.

The Israeli military claimed it was targeting Hezbollah after the Iran-backed group struck its soldiers in the south overnight. The army said it struck Hezbollah “weapon storage facilities”.

“Israel targeted the town of Arab Salim in the Nabatieh governorate. It targeted a residential area,” said Al Jazeera’s Zeina Khodr, reporting from Beirut about the deadly strike.

“The Israeli army says it is hitting infrastructure, and that this is in retaliation for Hezbollah launching armed drones at its forces in the Ali al-Taher ridge overnight.

“It’s not the first time the Israeli army accuses Hezbollah of targeting its forces in this area, which overlooks the city of Nabatieh’s strategic high ground, which really remains contested territory. We know that the Israeli army wants Hezbollah to vacate this area, so we’re seeing this increase in military pressure,” she said.

According to Israel, Iran-backed fighters “launched two explosive drones” towards Israeli soldiers operating in the Ali al-Taher ridge, but there were no casualties.

Israel has stepped up its strikes on south Lebanon in recent days, following an August 15 wave of strikes that Lebanon said killed 11 people, including several children. Israel’s military said the raids were retaliation for a Hezbollah attack.

Al Jazeera’s Khodr said that while “there has been a reduction in the violence in recent days, we have also witnessed an escalation by the Israeli army”.

“There is growing concern that the [Israeli] army may broaden this offensive, and it may become even more intense,” she added.

Tensions between Israel and Lebanon have been escalating since Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023. Lebanon was dragged into the conflict on March 2, days after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. Hezbollah struck Israel in support of Tehran. This was followed by massive Israeli air strikes and a ground invasion that Lebanese authorities say have killed more than 4,300 people.

The continued strikes have renewed debate in Beirut over the “framework” agreement Lebanon signed with Israel in June, which envisages a phased Israeli withdrawal in exchange for the deployment of the Lebanese army and the disarmament of armed groups, a reference to Hezbollah.

articles.title: Selena Gomez asks judge to dismiss ‘absurd’ fraud lawsuit over Wondermind mental health startup
articles.summary: Selena Gomez is fighting back against a federal lawsuit alleging she defrauded investors in Wondermind, the mental health startup she co-founded with her mother.
articles.body: Selena Gomez is fighting back against a federal lawsuit alleging she defrauded investors in Wondermind, the mental health startup she co-founded with her mother. In a motion filed in Delaware federal court on Wednesday, Gomez’s lawyers asked a judge to dismiss a lawsuit brought by investors of Wondermind, who allege they were misled into investing nearly $1.2 million in the 2021 start-up after being made false promises about the company’s leadership, resources, and infrastructure for years. The lawsuit, filed for common-law fraud, breach of contract, and securities fraud, names Gomez, her mother, Mandy Teefey, and their former business partner, Daniella Pierson. “The notion that Selena engaged in ‘fraud’ or any other wrongdoing is absurd — and in addition to filing our motion we are exploring other avenues of relief for Ms. Gomez including sanctions against plaintiffs for improperly including her,” Mathew S. Rosengart, an attorney for Gomez, said in a statement to NBC News. Wondermind and Teefey did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Pierson, who has previously denied any wrongdoing, also did not respond to a request for comment. According to the complaint — filed on Aug. 13 in federal court in Delaware by Wondermind SRS 44 LLC and Bespoke Wondermind SPV I LLC, limited liability companies that invested in the startup — the three founders allegedly told investors the sprawling “mental fitness” company would include a phone app, advertising deals and celebrity-driven content with Gomez “intimately involved” as head of marketing. Instead, the complaint alleges that many of those initiatives never happened, that investors received false updates, and that they were kept in the dark about Wondermind’s mismanagement and descent into financial turmoil. It alleges investors became aware of the company’s disarray after two bombshell stories by Forbes and The Cut. Gomez’s attorneys, however, argue in the motion that the lawsuit does not specify any false statements the singer made personally to investors and that she was not even a member of the board. The motion added that Gomez never agreed to manage Wondermind and did not hold a minority stake in the company. The “vague, generalized, and contradictory allegations concerning Selena Gomez demonstrate that Ms. Gomez could not possibly have engaged in any ‘fraud’ (she did not), is not liable to Plaintiffs (she is not) and, as a matter of law, must be dismissed from this lawsuit,” the motion states. The motion notes that Teefy and Pierson handled management as Wondermind’s co-CEOs and board members, and Gomez was retained “as a consultant and conferred on her title of Chief Impact Officer.” It notes that one of the few communications cited in the lawsuit that directly involved Gomez was a December 2022 email from Pierson discussing Wondermind’s growth. Gomez was copied on the email, according to the court filings, and her lawyers argue that there is no allegation she knew anything in it was false. The motion asks the judge to dismiss all four claims brought against Gomez with prejudice. Rosengart added in a statement that the “motion to dismiss demonstrates that plaintiffs never should have dragged Selena Gomez into this case as the claims against her are completely meritless if not frivolous.” In a statement to NBC News earlier this month, Pierson says she categorically denied the allegations and said she “welcomes the opportunity to present concrete documentation and financial records that establish the facts.” “To be clear, she has never used investor funds for personal expenses. Quite the opposite: Daniella invested her own money into the business and did not draw a salary from the company,” she said in a statement.

articles.title: Woman Baffled After She Finds Photo of Herself for Sale at a Thrift Shop (Exclusive)
articles.summary: Ansley Martin tells PEOPLE her family was “crying laughing” after the decades-old portrait unexpectedly turned up an hour from where she grew up
articles.body:
Ansley Martin's sister's friend spotted an old portrait of her family at a thrift store about an hour from where she grew up

The photo once hung in Ansley's childhood home, but neither of her parents donated it and her family still doesn't know how it got there

Ansley chose not to buy the portrait because she has better family photos, but it later disappeared from the sales floor

Ansley Martin's parents have been divorced for 15 years, but somehow, an old portrait of the family was still together — sitting inside a thrift store an hour away from where she grew up. Stranger still, no one in her family had any idea how it got there.

"My sister's friend actually spotted the picture first about a week prior, and sent her a hilarious text saying she found a picture that was really giving 'Ansley and Amelia' vibes," Ansley tells PEOPLE. Once the family realized what her friend had stumbled across, Ansley says she, her sister and her mom got on FaceTime and were "literally crying laughing."

Ansley eventually went to see the portrait herself, a moment shared on TikTok with the text, "found my family portrait at a random thrift store an hour away from my house but my parents have been divorced for 15 years and no one knows how it got here." In the caption, she summed up the family's reaction even more simply: "we're all very confused."

The portrait was instantly recognizable because Ansley had spent years looking at it in her childhood home. In fact, it had been such a fixture that she never noticed when it disappeared, and she had assumed it was still somewhere in the basement.

Her mom didn't remember getting rid of it either, leaving the family with more questions than answers. "Everyone is still so confused and bamboozled by the mystery," Ansley says. "It's become a running joke."

The family considered whether the photo studio could have produced another copy, but they haven't been able to confirm that theory. Their current guess is that someone was more interested in what was around the photo than the photo itself: "Our running theory is someone wanted the frame and donated it," she says.

There was, however, one part of the mystery Ansley had already settled: She wasn't bringing the portrait home. When a TikTok commenter wrote, "i hope you bought it," Ansley responded, "the thing is... i dont want it."

Her reasoning was considerably less sentimental than viewers might have expected. "Honestly it's just not that cute of a picture hahaha," Ansley says of the portrait, which she remembers being taken during a church photo shoot around 2002.

She already has plenty of old family photos she likes better, and after seeing this particular one throughout her childhood, she didn't feel the need to add it back into the collection. "This one feels permanently engrained in my brain from looking at it for so much of my childhood," she says.

Instead, Ansley told the thrift store employees that the strangers whose lives they had been imagining were actually her family. By then, the employees had already been giving the people in the portrait fake names and backstories, and Ansley says everyone got a kick out of finally learning who they were.

One employee even suggested taking the portrait off the sales floor and hanging it in the back office now that they knew its history. That idea became more intriguing when a TikTok commenter said they went to the store a few days after Ansley posted the video and the portrait was no longer there.

Whether it ended up in the back office or went home with another shopper is yet another question Ansley can't answer. A month after posting the TikTok, she says neither parent donated the photo and the rest of the family remains just as clueless about how it made its unlikely journey.

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer​​, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

Ansley is happy, however, that it surfaced at Philly AIDS Thrift, which she says supports local communities affected by HIV/AIDS. She calls it an "iconic Philadelphia institution" and is glad the strange discovery has made other people laugh as much as it made her family and friends laugh.

If a stranger really did buy a portrait of a family they've never met, Ansley is perfectly fine with that too. "I'm not creeped out by the situation, I found the whole thing hilarious, and thought leaving it there was just way funnier than taking it home myself."

articles.title: How California is preparing for Donald Trump’s midterm election scrutiny
articles.summary: Trump has accused the state of ‘cheating’. But election officials say they are using outreach to combat misinformation.
articles.body:
San Francisco, California – In May, as the midterm election season began to heat up, United States President Donald Trump turned his eye to a frequent target: California.

Speaking to Fox News, the Republican leader painted a picture of the left-leaning state as a chaotic free-for-all with no safeguards for voting integrity.

"California is very fraud [sic]. The whole thing is a fraud. The whole deal: Their elections are a fraud. Their mail-in votes are a fraud," Trump told Fox News host Lara Trump, his daughter-in-law.

"You know, they don't have voting booths. Everything's by mail," he added.

None of those assertions are true. But as November's general election approaches, Trump has continued to raise unfounded concerns about election integrity, particularly in states like California, where Democrats are expected to notch wins.

Voting officials in the state, however, say they are prepared to confront the scrutiny.

“At the end of the day, part of our job is to be transparent and instil confidence within the public about our processes," said Matt Moreles, the registrar of voters in Santa Clara County, which encompasses the city of San Jose.

While contingency plans are in place if Trump seeks to change the state's elections, Moreles explained that his office is investing primarily in voter education.

“That’s really where we’re focusing our efforts: making sure we're providing clear and consistent messaging that cuts through all of the misinformation or disinformation that’s floating out there," he said.

articles.title: In 1776, a Gettysburg minister built his stone home; 200 years later a young couple saved it from demolition, and today the city's oldest building is marking its 250th birthday
articles.summary: US News: Gettysburg's oldest surviving building, the 1776 Dobbin House, marked its 250th anniversary on Wednesday, 26 August 2026, celebrating two and a half c.
articles.body: Gettysburg's oldest surviving building, the 1776 Dobbin House, marked its 250th anniversary on Wednesday, 26 August 2026, celebrating two and a half centuries since Irish-born Presbyterian minister Reverend Alexander Dobbin completed the stone home. The anniversary was marked with a public reenactment of Dobbin's original 1776 consecration ceremony at 89 Steinwehr Avenue. According to local news outlet Gettysburg Connection, the event included living history presentations, colonial music, self-guided tours and a formal blessing to dedicate the building for another 250 years. The building was completed in the same year the United States declared independence. Rev. Dobbin built it as a family home and classical school. Over the years, it became a tavern, a stop on the Underground Railroad and a field hospital during the Battle of Gettysburg in 1863.Saved from possible demolitionDespite its long history, the building nearly disappeared before reaching its 200th birthday. By the 1970s, years of use, weather damage and neglect had left the stone structure in poor condition and at risk of being demolished. The building was saved when local couple Jacqueline and Gary White took over the property in the mid-1970s. They began a major restoration that included strengthening the foundation, repairing the fieldstone walls, restoring hand-carved woodwork and rebuilding seven working fireplaces. "By the 1970s, the Dobbin House stood at the brink of loss—weathered, neglected, and facing possible demolition," said current owner Jacqueline White in historical material published by the Dobbin House Tavern. The couple turned the historic home into a colonial-style tavern and restaurant, which opened to the public in 1978. The rooms were carefully decorated in an eighteenth-century style, with china and flatware chosen to match historical items found during cellar excavations. Many of the antique furnishings still inside the house are similar to objects listed in Rev. Dobbin's original 1809 estate inventory.New public museum spaceThe 250th anniversary celebrations will continue throughout the week. On Saturday, 29 August 2026, a public dedication will mark the opening of three permanent additions to the site, including the new Dobbin House Square. The outdoor educational museum and public gathering space on Steinwehr Avenue will offer free access to historical displays around the clock. The square includes full-size settings of the "Charters of Freedom", featuring permanent replicas of the Declaration of Independence, the United States Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the Civil Rights Amendments and the Gettysburg Address. The displays were donated through the Forward Foundation. "Dobbin House Square will ensure this historic area continues to inspire future generations with five life-size Charters of Freedom settings," representatives said in a statement published by Gettysburg Connection. "The park is dedicated to preserving the past while investing in its future." Saturday's programme will include an honour guard led by the 1st Pennsylvania Volunteer Cavalry Fife & Drum Corps and Spencer's Additional Continental Regiment. The event will end with a seven-gun cannon salute. Reenactors will present living history programmes during the afternoon, followed by Celtic music performances in the evening and historical films projected onto the stone walls of the house.A building with centuries of historyHistorical records show how the Dobbin House changed with the needs of the local community across four centuries. When Rev. Dobbin built the house in 1776, it served as both his family home and the Alexander Dobbin Classical School. The academy educated some of the area's early lawyers, doctors and political leaders and became known as one of the first higher education institutions west of the Susquehanna River. Before the American Civil War, the property also became a secret stop on the Underground Railroad. Freedom seekers escaping slavery could find temporary shelter in hidden spaces built into the upper parts of the house. During the Battle of Gettysburg in July 1863, the building's strong stone walls provided shelter near the fighting. Surgeons also used the house as a temporary field hospital, treating wounded Union and Confederate soldiers as fighting spread across the surrounding area. Today, the historic property operates as a commercial site with the Springhouse Tavern, Alexander Dobbin Fine Dining Rooms, Abigail Adams Ballroom and Gettystown Inn bed and breakfast. Located near the entrance to Gettysburg National Cemetery, the restored building remains an important part of tourism in Adams County and a lasting reminder of the area's history.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
