articles.title: Lindsay Clancy trial in hands of jury after closing arguments conclude
articles.summary: Prosecutors argued Clancy made a calculated decision to murder the children, while the defence argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.
articles.body:
Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

The fate of US mother Lindsay Clancy is now in the hands of a Massachusetts jury, who must decide if she is guilty of first-degree murder - the intentional and premeditated killing of another person - in the deaths of her three children.

For five weeks, the trial has gripped the country as Clancy's lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, who ranged in age from eight months to five years. Clancy does not deny killing her two sons and daughter.

The prosecution argued she made a calculated decision to intentionally murder them.

The jury could find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of lesser charges, or not guilty.

The jury of nine women and three men completed their first day of deliberations on Thursday. They will return on Friday.

In the state of Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory life in prison sentence without the possibility of parole.

The jury could instead find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or involuntary manslaughter - causing death because of extreme carelessness. Those convictions, too, would lead to some prison time.

If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, then she will not be set free, but instead sent to a psychiatric hospital, where she possibly could remain for life.

Key moments in trial of Lindsay Clancy, the mother accused of murdering her three children

Attorneys for both sides made closing arguments on Thursday before the jury began deliberating.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, repeated the defence's argument that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children with exercise bands at their home and then attempted to end her own life by jumping out of a window. Clancy was paralysed by the attempt and has attended the trial in a wheelchair.

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect," Reddington said, adding that he believed prosecutors were "not going to be able to prove otherwise".

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare and serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, and which should be treated as a medical emergency.

One of the more tense moments of the closing arguments came when Reddington directly addressed the prosecutors and asked them to explain why they tried to prove Clancy's suicide attempt was not serious. The judge interrupted and ordered him to address only the jury.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague did not dispute that Clancy was mentally ill, but told the jury that the defendant could tell the difference between right and wrong at the time of the killings.

"It's not the system or the DSM that caused her to strangle her kids," Sprague told the jury, referencing the US encyclopedia of mental heath diagnoses, which does not give postpartum psychosis its own classification.

Sprague also said Clancy had an "abundance of care", but had hidden thoughts from doctors about harming her kids.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide.

In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

articles.title: A London apartment burned down in 2024 and left more than 80 people homeless; two years later, one owner says she is still paying the mortgage on a home that no longer exists
articles.summary: UK News: Former residents of a London apartment block destroyed in a major fire are still paying monthly mortgages on homes that were reduced to rubble two yea.
articles.body: Former residents of a London apartment block destroyed in a major fire are still paying monthly mortgages on homes that were reduced to rubble two years ago. The fire at the seven-storey Spectrum Building on Freshwater Road in Dagenham started in the early hours of 26 August 2024. More than 80 people were forced to leave their homes and four were injured. Scaffolding around the former office block, which had been put up to remove unsafe cladding using a £5.9 million government grant, helped the flames spread quickly. The building suffered such serious structural damage that it was later demolished, leaving homeowners without a physical property.A report by ITV News London on 26 August 2026 found that affected leaseholders are still stuck in financial uncertainty. Banks continue to collect mortgage payments even though the building no longer exists, while insurance claims remain tied up in complicated legal and financial processes. "We still haven't got our money, and we have no idea whether it will even cover the value of the flats," said Sarah Williams, a charity worker who bought her apartment in 2016, in an interview with ITV News London. "We've still got to pay our mortgages. We've still got to pay our rent."Insolvency delays insurance paymentsThe financial situation became more complicated after the building's freeholder, Arinium Ltd, went into administration following the fire. Financial consultancy firm FRP was appointed to manage the company's assets and deal with insurance claims. According to updates from PropertyWire, insurance policies cover temporary emergency accommodation for displaced leaseholders for up to three years. Residents are worried about what will happen when that period ends if their final compensation has not yet been paid. FRP administrators have asked the court for permission to begin distributing the first round of insurance payments to leaseholders and creditors. The firm has described the case as "incredibly complex", saying it needs special valuation methods and independent legal advice to work out how much each person should receive. In a statement, FRP said that dealing with insurance payments was one of its main responsibilities. However, the administrators have no control over private mortgage agreements between residents and banks. Former residents have also faced further demands for money. An investigation by housing publication Inside Housing found that managing agents had sent bills for unpaid service charges dating back to 2021. Some two-bedroom properties were being charged as much as £2,130, despite the homes no longer existing.Government faces pressure over building safetyThe continuing problems faced by Spectrum Building residents have increased scrutiny of Britain's building safety policies. After the 2024 fire, then-Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner visited the Dagenham site. She criticised the slow removal of dangerous cladding across the UK and promised government action to speed up safety work. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) also said urgent action was needed. "Former residents of Spectrum building must be fairly and urgently compensated for their losses, and it is for the administrator to make sure that they get any money they are rightfully owed," an MHCLG spokesperson said. "Our interest is getting back taxpayers' money that was not used for its intended purpose – and this does not supersede the interests of the residents." Campaigners say the wider building safety crisis has still not been properly addressed. Data from End Our Cladding Scandal showed that the share of unsafe buildings where cladding work had either started or been completed increased only from 50 per cent to 53 per cent during the two years after the Dagenham fire. "It feels like Labour prioritised building 1.5m homes, and that's meant they've swept ending the building safety crisis under the carpet," said Giles Grover of End Our Cladding Scandal, according to PropertyWire.Dispute over government fundingFormer residents also faced more uncertainty after the Greater London Authority registered an interest as a possible creditor in the administration of Arinium Ltd. The authority is seeking to recover any unused part of the £5.9 million government grant that had been given for cladding removal through the Building Safety Fund. The Ministry of Housing later issued a clarification on its official media blog, saying the claim was a normal step under UK insolvency law. The department said taxpayers' money would only be recovered if money remained after leaseholders had received full market compensation for their lost homes and belongings. For residents such as Jesse Gill, however, the explanation has done little to ease the financial pressure. Gill moved into the Spectrum Building with his wife only two weeks before the fire destroyed their flat. "We haven't been reimbursed our ground rent or service charges, and we're having to pay our mortgage for a property that doesn't exist," Gill told reporters. Although the London Fire Brigade has completed its technical investigation into the structural failures at Freshwater Road, former residents remain caught between banks, insurers and administrators. Two years after the fire, they continue to make monthly mortgage payments on homes that are no longer there.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: US man arrested with gun near Trump’s LA golf course sent for mental health evaluation
articles.summary: US News: A California judge has suspended criminal proceedings against a former US Marine who was arrested near President Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf .
articles.body: A California judge has suspended criminal proceedings against a former US Marine who was arrested near President Donald Trump’s Los Angeles-area golf course with a loaded gun and ammunition, ordering him to undergo a mental health evaluation.Jeanine John Taele, 38, was arrested on August 5, days before Trump was scheduled to attend a Republican National Committee dinner at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes.According to news agency AP, Taele was found with a loaded 9mm pistol, binoculars and a badge identifying him as a “security protection agent”.Los Angeles County Judge John Lonergan Jr. ruled Wednesday that Taele was not mentally fit to stand trial and sent him to a mental health court in Hollywood for evaluation. Taele will remain in custody and is due to appear before the mental health court on September 9.Taele faces several felony charges, including possession of a short-barrelled rifle or shotgun and receiving a large-capacity magazine. He also faces a misdemeanor charge of carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle.Prosecutors said Taele had been spotted at the golf course on July 31 wearing an earpiece and taking photographs and videos. He returned two days later, prompting golf club staff to alert federal security personnel.A search of his pickup truck reportedly uncovered the loaded pistol, ammunition and binoculars.Investigators later found firearms, body armour, high-capacity magazines, radio equipment and notebooks containing what authorities described as concerning statements at his home.The Guardian reported that Taele appeared in court wearing a suicide-prevention gown, while his attorney argued that he was unable to understand or participate in the proceedings.Lonergan also expressed concern over about 200 pages of writings investigators recovered. The documents reportedly included schedules for first lady Melania Trump and Secret Service members, as well as detailed plans for surviving “off the grid”.Taele previously served in the US Marines and was deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan between 2008 and 2016.He was a decorated corporal who received several military honours, according to a Marine Corps spokesperson.The case comes nearly two years after Ryan Routh was convicted of attempting to assassinate Trump at his Florida golf club in September 2024. Routh was sentenced to life in prison in February.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'I stopped all my internet accounts': 70-year-old Australian man falls in love with six-fingered deepfake, transfers $180,000
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A retired psychologist in his 70s has been scammed out of $180,000 while he believed he had found his soulmate online. Queensland's Michael continued .
articles.body: A retired psychologist in his 70s has been scammed out of $180,000 while he believed he had found his soulmate online. Queensland's Michael continued his long-distance courtship with Melanie, a nurse in South Africa, until she turned out to be a deepfake with six fingers and distorted AI video after a year. Michael and Melanie met over a dating app and Michael told A Current Affair that he had his doubts initially but Melanie shared her passport, identity card and nurse registration certificate.“She said she was only about 50 years of age, and getting somebody interested [in me], it was obviously flattering,” Michael told A Current Affair.“My head said, this can’t be true, but my heart said I don’t want to abandon her.”Voice cloning, face-swappingDr Priyanka Singh, a specialist in digital forensics at the University of Queensland, analyzed the final 10-minute break-up video call between the pair after it was proved that there was no Melanie in real. She pointed out that there were slight distortions in the woman's earrings, the chair in which Melanie was sitting was changing shape and when Melanie brushed her face, she had six fingers.Scammers used the social media profile of an American doctor who had no knowledge of this fraud and combined this with her YouTube videos. They used voice cloning technology and the latest face-swapping applications to create a digital mask they used to put on every time Michael dialled in to make a video call.Then Melanie sought financial help from Michael and Michael handed $180,000 to the scammers despite warnings from his bank.Michael reported the case to New South Wales police, who conducted an investigation but concluded the scam was based overseas and it was unlikely he would recover the lost money. “I stopped all my internet accounts ... the best way is to meet somebody in person, isn’t it?” he said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘It’s death by scurvy’: Tristan and Andrew Tate seek bail as they fight extradition to United Kingdom
articles.summary: Attorneys for Andrew and Tristan Tate, the “manosphere” influencers accused of sex crimes in the United Kingdom, fought for their freedom on Thursday, telling a federal judge that the defendants are not a flight risk.
articles.body: MIAMI — Andrew and Tristan Tate, the “manosphere” influencers accused of sex crimes in the United Kingdom, told a judge Thursday that they’re not actually outrageous online personalities in real life. U.S. Magistrate Judge Lauren Louis will decide whether the men brothers, who are dual American and U.K. citizens, should be eligible for bail as they fight extradition across on charges of rape, sex trafficking and other crimes. They have denied the allegations. After Andrew Tate took the witness stand Thursday afternoon, he denied being a rapist or human trafficker and described the proceedings as his “last chance.” “If there’s any court in the world that will listen to me,” he testified, “it will be an American court.” Earlier, Tristian Tate told the judge that he was testifying against the advice of his defense attorneys and compared his and his brother’s online personas to actor Sacha Baron Cohen, the famed British Jewish comic best known for playing journalist Borat Sagdiyev. At one point, when Assistant U.S. Attorney Abbie Waxman asked Tristan Tate if he was a liar, the defendant responded: “I play a character, no more than any actor.” Tristan Tate said he spends his days locked in a 5-by-11 cell that has a bunk bed, a toilet and unwanted roommates. He said that he’d been subjected to chemical attacks and that his daily diet consists mostly of candy and chips. ”It’s death by scurvy instead of death by starvation.” The brothers, shackled and wearing beige jail garb on Thursday, were taken into custody in Miami in July after prosecutors in the United Kingdom filed new charges against them. Defense lawyer Howard Srebnick argued that his clients are not flight risks and have appeared “each and every time” for court dates in the U.K. and Romania. Their confinement poses an undue burden on the defendants, Srebnick said, adding that Tristan Tate has a child with special needs who depends on him. The pair have been unfairly cast as monsters for the internet “characters” they play, Srebnick said. Andrew Tate’s social media personality as “Top G” uses “foul language, speaks in vulgarities, advocates positions that are in many ways outrageous,” the lawyer conceded. But that internet personality “is not the real Andrew Tate — that is not the person Andrew Tate. That is the character,” Srebnick said. At the bail hearing, Andrew Tate’s girlfriend testified to his character. Natasha Sesay said she’s known Andrew Tate for about 5 1/2 years and they have a child who is 8 1/2 months old, and another one due in a month. “It’s a very different character from the person you see online versus the one I know personally,” Sesay told the court. “He’s a great father to his children.” Defense attorney Joe McBride has previously denied the allegations and said the brothers’ incarceration was the “result of an unholy alliance between the enemies of free speech in the United States and the United Kingdom.” McBride told the court Thursday that his clients are “running to the fight,” calling them “two innocent men who have shown up” in multiple jurisdictions to “face the music” and to “go on the offense.” “Innocent men don’t run. They lean into the process,” McBride added. Prosecutors in the U.K. had argued against their release, saying in a filing earlier this month that men’s own statements suggest they intended to evade justice. The filing also alleged they may seek to interfere with witnesses and said the brothers repeatedly sought the names of their accusers from prosecutors in exchange for a “security” fee worth tens of thousands of pounds and a promise not to publicly identify the accusers. The Crown Prosecution Service declined the offer in an effort to safeguard the complainants, the filing states. McBride said the filing “drips falsehood from every page.” A former professional kickboxer, Andrew Tate, 39, built a vast online following espousing misogynistic and hypermasculine views. He once told an interviewer that there was “no way you can be rooted in reality and not be sexist.” British prosecutors initially charged the Tates with 21 counts of rape, assault occasioning actual bodily harm and arranging or facilitating travel for sexual exploitation. Andrew Tate was also charged with controlling prostitution. The additional charges filed last month against Andrew Tate include seven counts of rape, 15 counts of making or distributing indecent images of children and four counts of possession of extreme pornography. Tristan Tate, 38, was charged with six additional counts of rape, sexual assault and sexual exploitation charges. U.K. authorities said the alleged crimes took place between 2010 and 2017. The brothers also face criminal charges in Romania, where they reportedly moved in 2016 to build an online porn business and were later indicted on allegations of forming an organized criminal group, human trafficking, trafficking of minors and money laundering. They have denied the charges. Juliette Arcodia reported from Miami, Tim Stelloh from San Francisco and David K. Li from New York City.

articles.title: Mali music star Salif Keïta cancels South African concerts over 'xenophobic violence'
articles.summary: He says his decision is "a rejection of hate" rather than a rejection of South Africans.
articles.body:
The decision by world-famous Malian musician Salif Keïta to stop touring in South Africa over what he called "xenophobic violence" has been met with disappointment by the province hosting a festival he was due to perform at next month.

South Africa has been hit by a wave of protests demanding that undocumented migrants leave the country - the latest unofficial deadline set is 30 September.

Tens of thousands of Africans have been voluntarily repatriated in recent months, some saying they have been the targets of intimidation and attacks.

While cracking down on illegal immigration, the South African government has said that those who have taken the law into their own hands have been arrested.

South Africa is Africa's wealthiest nation and has long attracted migrants searching for better economic opportunities.

But illegal immigration has become a highly contentious political issue, with protesters accusing undocumented migrants of placing pressure on South Africa's public services, as well as being involved in crime.

'They came with machetes' - deadline looms for migrants to leave South Africa

In a message explaining why he would not be performing at the Macufe festival in Free State province next month, Keïta said he could not "ignore the reports of xenophobic violence against our African brothers and sisters.

"When I see migrants attacked, I do not see 'politics'. I see people looking for work, safety, and dignity."

The 77-year-old star added that this did not reflect the country that he knew and that cancelling the appearance was "a rejection of hate" rather than a rejection of South Africans, leaving the door open for a return at some point.

In its response, the Free State's culture department said it "regrets the decision taken by the renowned musician".

It emphasised that the Macufe festival was a celebration of African unity.

Keïta, known to some as the "Golden Voice of Africa", was a pioneer who helped put African music on the global map and after 50 years in the music business remains influential.

News of the cancellation of his concert came as the first group of 173 Tanzanians returned from South Africa as part of a voluntary repatriation programme.

For some of them the flight home from Durban, which has seen some of the biggest protests, marks the end of decades spent in South Africa.

Abdul Idi, who went there in 2006 hoping to build a better life, said he was grateful to have returned safely after what he described as difficult and dangerous circumstances in South Africa.

"Foreigners are not wanted there," he said on arrival at Dar es Salaam's international airport on Wednesday night.

Another returnee, Rashid Ramadhan, said he had spent 30 years in South Africa.

The 53-year-old explained how he and others had been forced out of their accommodation in Durban and had been living outside for the past two months, with their jobs gone and life becoming increasingly difficult.

More than 160,000 people have left the country on similar repatriation schemes since May, according to a count by the AFP news agency. Malawians, Zimbabweans, Zambians, Ghanaians and Nigerians are among those who have returned.

The anti-migrant group March and March has announced a second wave of nationwide protests set for 30 September.

Earlier this month, the group called on leaders attending the Southern African Development Community (Sadc) summit in Durban to "fetch your people".

March and March says its September action will be bigger and better organised than the demonstrations on 30 June, which were accompanied by violence in some areas.

Those returning to their home countries from South Africa often need support, having abandoned their livelihoods and many of their possessions.

But Ghana's government has rejected a donation of about $1.7m (£1.25m) from MTN Ghana, a subsidiary of South African telecoms giant MTN Group, offered to support Ghanaians repatriated from South Africa.

Ghana's foreign ministry said that the government was committed to funding the evacuation and reintegration of its repatriated citizens.

articles.title: France relaxes strict cheese-making rules after prolonged drought
articles.summary: Makers of some of France's most famous cheeses get waivers on where herds graze due to the lack of grass.
articles.body:
France has temporarily relaxed rules for making some of its best-known cheeses after the summer drought drastically reduced the amount of grass available to feed milk herds.

Government decrees to grant dispensations to manufacturers of Abondance, Beaufort and Comté cheeses - which come from mountains in eastern France - appeared on Wednesday.

Several other cheeses are expected to receive similar waivers, allowing farmers to feed livestock with grass and hay brought in from outside their strict geographical zone.

These include Cantal, Bleu d'Auvergne, Fourme d'Ambert, Bleu du Vercors-Sassenage, Reblochon and the goats cheese Rocamadour.

The National Institute for Origin and Quality (INAO), which regulates France's labels of origin, has also approved temporary changes to the rules for other protected produce because of the effects of the summer heat.

Products that will benefit include some types of Calvados and cider from Normandy, Crémant d'Alsace fizzy wine, lamb from Poitou-Charentes, and Reine-Claude plums.

Certificates of origin allow farmers to sell at a premium, but they come with strict regulations governing the location and method of production.

The aim is to preserve the unique identity of cheeses, wines and other foodstuffs, supposedly linked to their particular terroir - a French concept that links locality and tradition.

Because of a 2026 drought - which the INAO now describes as "historic" - farmers are being allowed to bend the rules for a short period.

Makers of Abondance cheese in the Alps, for example, will be authorised to reduce the amount of pastured grass in their animals' diet from 50% to 15%. They will be entitled to import forage from outside their zone, and use some supplements.

Makers of Comté cheese in the Jura mountains will be able to replace the local green maize they usually give to their cattle with maize from elsewhere.

The derogations are allowed in French and European law for periods of exceptional weather. Similar measures came in after the dry summer of 2022.

It will be interesting to see if the changes lead to any detectable change in the taste or quality of the cheeses - or to the quantity produced and how it is priced.

Longer term, the measures raise questions over the viability of the existing labels of origin in France and elsewhere.

If changing climate means that certain foodstuffs can no longer be produced in their traditional localities, then the idea of terroir will be stretched to its limits.

articles.title: 'My sister is missing since Nepal's flash floods'
articles.summary: Hundreds of people have died after a catastrophic natural disaster near the Nepal-Tibet border.
articles.body:
A woman says she has not been able to contact her sister who was near the Nepal-Tibet border when devastating flash flooding hit.

Nepalese authorities reported at least 389 people have died and more than 900 are missing, including 33 UK tourists, following the natural disaster on Wednesday.

In Tibet, at least 558 people are missing, with three confirmed dead, but it is unclear if these figures overlap with Nepal's.

Tatajana Phillips, from Folkestone in Kent, said the last known location of her sister Julija Jakovicka was in the border area an hour before the flash floods struck.

"Then there is no more news," she told the BBC.

"We are really hoping that people hear us and try to find and locate [my sister]".

Phillips said her sister, a mother-of-two living in Germany, was in the country for a yoga and meditation retreat.

"We are terribly worried," added Phillips's husband Ben. "We just know where they were and that's really tough."

It comes as members of the Nepalese community in Kent have sent messages of hope and comfort to those impacted by the flash floods.

Medway Council's Nina Gurung, who is a representative of the Gurkha-Nepalese community, told BBC Radio Kent the situation was "absolutely shocking and devastating".

Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border

"We are trying to get further updates from families and friends back home to support each other and see what we can do here in the UK," she said.

Despite the overwhelming situation, Gurung added the community was doing whatever it could to show solidarity and send out a message to those impacted to "stay strong".

"We heard reports entire villages have been wiped out, impacting infrastructure including communications," Gurung continued.

"I think because communications have been cut off, it has hampered rescue efforts."

Gurung said there was a glimmer of hope as survivors were "being pulled out waist-deep from mud".

"We pray for all those who lost their lives and we offer our heartfelt sympathy and condolences to the families of those who died", she added.

"We also pray for those who are still missing to be found safe, including those who are from the UK."

Flash floods caused rivers to burst their banks and spread thick mud across populated areas, burying houses and creating difficult conditions for rescuers.

Videos posted on social media showed flood waters surging through valleys as people screamed in terror, with bridges being washed away.

Other videos showed people desperately fleeing uphill to escape the surging waters.

It means taking down all five members of the opposing team, so getting four kills and being one hit away from the fifth makes the final elimination especially important.That was exactly where Tyler1 found himself during the game. He had already taken down several opponents and was moving toward the last kill when MoistCr1TiKaL stepped in and secured it himself.Tyler1 immediately reacted.“What is wrong with you, bro? You’re never being invited back ever again. Ever again. Ever again, boy. You’ll never come back. I’ll never talk to you again in my life, by the way. Who does that? Who does that?” he said.The reaction was classic Tyler1, but MoistCr1TiKaL did not seem too worried. Instead of giving a serious explanation, he admitted that he simply saw the chance and took it.“I couldn’t help myself. The opportunity was just laid bare before me,” MoistCr1TiKaL said.That might have been the end of it if it had happened only once. But the same situation came up again later, making Tyler1’s frustration even more understandable.Why did Tyler1 call MoistCr1TiKaL a “psycho” after the second kill?When another potential pentakill slipped away, Tyler1 reacted even more strongly.“What the f*** is wrong with you, boy? You’re f***ing psycho, bro,” he said.The second incident made the whole exchange funnier because MoistCr1TiKaL had already seen how annoyed Tyler1 was after the first one. Yet he still ended up taking another kill.Clips of the match were shared online, where viewers joined in with their own jokes. One person wrote, “If it can be taken from you, it was never really yours.”Another viewer simply joked, “loool, kill secured.”The clips also fit Tyler1’s reputation as a streamer who is rarely quiet when something goes wrong in a League of Legends game. His reactions have become a major part of his streams, and this time his own teammate gave him a reason to lose his patience.The incident was not the first time Tyler1 had recently been frustrated after a teammate secured a kill he wanted. Another clip from a game involving xQc also showed Tyler1 reacting after xQc landed the final hit on an enemy they were both attacking.That moment happened several days before the MoistCr1TiKaL game and created another example of Tyler1 watching a kill disappear just before he could claim it.Still, the MoistCr1TiKaL situation had an extra layer because it happened twice in the same game. The first steal annoyed Tyler1. The second one turned the whole thing into a running joke.For MoistCr1TiKaL, the reason was simple: he saw an opportunity and took it. For Tyler1, however, the missing pentakill was a little harder to laugh off.In the end, there was no serious argument between the two. articles.title: Severe weather, flooding threat hits Northeast: Forecast
articles.summary: Heavy thunderstorms could bring rainfall rates topping 2 inches per hour.
articles.body:
More than 38 million people from New York City to Washington, D.C., could face severe weather on Thursday afternoon and evening, including flash flooding, damaging winds, large hail and possible tornadoes.

The threat covers a wide swath of the Northeast, stretching from Syracuse, New York, and Vermont down to Virginia.

Along the Interstate 95 corridor from New York City to D.C., rainfall rates could top 2 inches per hour and rain totals could reach 5 inches in some areas.

A severe thunderstorm watch is in effect in New Jersey, New York City, parts of Long Island, Philadelphia, and Dover, Delaware, through 8 p.m. A flood watch is also in effect for the region.

The weather may cause flight disruptions at New York City's John F. Kennedy Airport, airport officials warned. At nearby LaGuardia Airport, over 100 flights have been canceled and more than 200 have been delayed.

articles.title: Zambia opposition leader questioned over ‘treason’ amid election fallout
articles.summary: Zambia’s entire judiciary closed on Monday on the last valid day to file a court challenge against Hichilema’s victory.
articles.body:
Zambia’s main opposition leader Brian Mundubile, who was runner-up in this month’s disputed presidential election, is being questioned by police over alleged treason.

⁠Mundubile and his running mate, Makebi Zulu, are in police custody after ⁠being questioned “in connection with an alleged offence of treason”, the Zambia Police ⁠Service said on Thursday.

Zambian state media said Mundubile surrendered to police in Lusaka on August 27, after spending two weeks at an international human rights organisation, where he sought safety after a police raid at his home the day after the country’s August 13 elections.

The two were interviewed by a team of police officers alongside their lawyers. Police did not immediately provide further details of the allegations underpinning the treason investigation. They said that “warn and caution” statements ⁠had been recorded, a ⁠step typically preceding formal charges.

Treason is a serious offence in ⁠Zambia and carries severe penalties upon conviction.

The developments follow an escalation from two weeks ago, during which former cabinet minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot and killed during the police crackdown in which 11 people were arrested at Mundubile’s home.

Police said the group were involved in alleged insurrection or militia activity, an accusation Mundubile has denied.

President Hakainde Hichilema won 60 percent of the vote and is due to be sworn in as president for a second term on Tuesday. The election results were disputed by opposition leaders.

Uncertainty over opposition election challenge

Mundubile, who won about 38 percent of the vote, promised to challenge the result in court, but Zambia closed its entire judiciary on Monday, the last day for filing an objection, citing “security reasons”.

Under Article 103 of the Zambian Constitution, an election petition must be filed within seven days of the winner being declared.

Filing the challenge automatically pauses the presidential swearing-in under Article 104.

Shutting the courts before that seven-day deadline expired physically blocked the opposition from filing, preventing the automatic pause on the inauguration.

The Constitutional Court said on Tuesday it had not received any petition challenging the election outcome, clearing the way for Hichilema to be sworn into office.

However, Chief Justice Mumba Malila said he had received a petition from a member of the public on his private email address.

He called the submission “highly irregular” but said he had referred it to the Constitutional Court for consideration.

Legal and rights groups have criticised the timing of the abrupt closure of the courts.

Human Rights Watch (HRW) said it was “a blow to the administration of law, transparency, and due process in Zambia”.

Concerns raised over shrinking of democratic space

Hichilema entered the race as the clear favourite after steering Zambia, Africa’s second-largest copper producer, through a major economic turnaround and restructuring its debt.

Opposition parties and civil society organisations have raised concerns over increasing repression by Hichilema’s government.

Rights groups and election observer missions have said the post-election dispute has tarnished Zambia’s democratic reputation.

Every change of president since the return to multiparty politics in 1991 has been achieved through elections.
